30236-pepita-ximenez:
Juan Valera's Pepita Ximenez comes in English from the Spanish, with an introduction by the author written specially for the Appleton edition of New York in 1886. Valera's preface to the American edition, addressed to the Messrs. Appleton, tells why he almost wrote no preface at all. He recalls a gallant who sought a presentation at a rich man's magnificent ball through a friend boasting familiarity with the great man.

The gallant won his introduction, only for the great man to ask the introducer who would introduce him, since they were not acquainted. Valera, professing respect and affection for America, refuses the introducer's bold answer that he needs no one, since he is just going away. From his story's evident moral, he draws restraint, letting the novel speak for itself in its first American dress.
30316-velazquez:
S. L. Bensusan presents Velazquez in the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by T. Leman Hare, with eight reproductions in colour. Jack of London and Stokes of New York published the volume in 1907, and the Infante Don Fernando of Austria fronts the book from the Prado in Madrid. Painted for the Torre de la Parada, the picture shows King Philip's younger brother in hunting costume, with part of the canvas repainted by Velazquez himself.

Other plates give Las Meniñas, the Infante Philip Prosper in Vienna, the Infante Don Balthasar Carlos, Antonio the Englishman, and Donna Mariana of Austria, all largely from the Prado. Admiral Adriano Pulido Pareja appears from the National Gallery in London, and the Princess Maria Theresa closes the set. Bensusan opens with a curious truth: Spain in decline still holds the world's mind almost as in her power.
3718-george-walker-at-suez:
Anthony Trollope gives this comic tale to George Walker, a small London clerk who stops at Suez on his way through Egypt. Walker calls Suez the vilest spot on earth, with no water, no women, and no green thing, only sand, sun, and a cavernous hotel stripped of comfort. Yet he owns a hankering after greatness, and dreams of being a popular orator or a man whom crowds must respect and perhaps fear.

His great day comes when a stout dignitary in a turban crosses the room straight toward him. Walker rises, bobs his head, rubs his hands, and ventures that it is a fine day. The comedy lies in his solemn pride at so small a triumph. Readers who enjoy first person bragging gently deflated will find Walker a frank and funny guide to his own vanity.
britannica-1911-aranjuez:
Aranjuez is a town of central Spain. It stands in the province of Madrid. The Tagus river flows past it. Madrid lies thirty miles north. Main southern railways junction there. Population in 1900 was 12,670. The town occupies a wide valley. That valley sits 1,500 feet above the sea. Formal straight streets cross at right angles.

Grimaldi directed the town's Dutch-style building. Uniform two-storeyed houses line the streets. A weir on the Tagus aids irrigation. An oasis results amid barren New Castile. Royal parks surround the town completely. Sycamores, planes, and elms grow huge there. Philip II introduced the dark English elms. They give the district a distinct character. Summer heat is oppressive, though. The climate is unhealthy despite the beauty. Spanish guide-books anchor the closing references.
britannica-1911-arbos-fernandez:
Fernández Arbós (1863– ) is a Spanish violinist and composer. Madrid was his birthplace. The Madrid conservatoire trained him first. Brussels continued his training afterwards. Berlin followed, under the master Joachim. He became a professor at Hamburg. Madrid later took him as professor too. Meanwhile his violin fame grew steadily. He ranked among the finest violinists of the day.

England received him in 1890. He established his reputation there firmly. The Royal College of Music made him professor. London thus gained a leading string teacher. Composition is his secondary fame. Violin pieces are his best-known works. A comic opera adds a stage credit. El Centro de la Tierra appeared in 1895. The entry is brief and purely biographical. It captures a performer at his reputation's height.
britannica-1911-bermudez:
Bermudez was a north-eastern state of Venezuela between the Caribbean Sea and the Orinoco River, bounded by the Gulf of Paria and the states of Guarico and Miranda. The 1911 Britannica entry, using a 1905 estimate of 364,158 people, explains that the state was formed in 1881 from Barcelona, Cumaná, and Maturín, dissolved in 1901, and reorganized in 1904.

Holding some of Venezuela's oldest settlements, the state had once prospered on cattle and hides, but wars and political disorder damaged its trades. Its main products were coffee, sugar, and cacao, with cotton, tobacco, coconuts, timber, and dyewoods behind them. Cumaná, founded in 1520, was its oldest town.
britannica-1911-carvajal-antonio-fernand:
Antonio Fernandez Carvajal (d. 1659) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Portuguese Marano, or crypto Jew, who came to England in the reign of Charles I. He was the first “endenizened” Jew in England, a formal grant of resident rights. His wide trade with the West Indies made him valuable to the Commonwealth, and he also served Cromwell as an “intelligencer,” a supplier of information.

When Manasseh ben Israel petitioned in 1655 for the return of the Jews expelled by Edward I, Carvajal joined the agitation and openly avowed his Judaism. The entry calls him the founder of the Anglo Jewish community, a title that rests on his standing as its first legal resident and public spokesman. He died in 1659. A cited paper by Lucien Wolf, “The First English Jew,” closes the short account for readers who want the evidence spelled out.
britannica-1911-ciudad-juarez:
Ciudad Juarez, formerly El Paso del Norte, is a northern frontier town of Mexico in Chihuahua, 1,223 miles by rail north-north-west of Mexico City. Its people numbered 6,917 in 1895, and it stands 3,800 feet above sea level on the right bank of the Rio Grande. Opposite lies El Paso, Texas, joined to it by two bridges. It is the northern terminus of the Mexican Central railway, with a custom house and a United States consulate.

Transit trade with the United States is large and increasing, and a small garrison makes it a military post. Houses are largely small adobe or brick cabins in a straggling, picturesque town. Nearby farms raise cattle and grow wheat, corn, fruit and grapes for wine and brandy. Founded in 1681 to 1682, it was President Juarez's headquarters in 1865 and took his name in 1885.
britannica-1911-coello-alonso-sanchez:
Alonso Sanchez Coello (1515–1590) was a Spanish painter whose birthplace is disputed. Some accounts make him a native of Portugal. Others place his birth at Benifacio, near Valencia. He studied for many years in Italy. He came back to Spain in 1541 and settled at Madrid. There he painted sacred themes for palaces and large churches.

He followed Titian and matched him in one strength. His portraits and single figures show fine care for surface detail. Armour, cloth and like gear are worked with masterly skill. That care left a mark on Velazquez and his handling of the same things. Fires in Madrid palaces destroyed many of his works. Survivors include portraits of the infantes Carlos and Isabella. His daughter Isabella studied under him and painted portraits well.
britannica-1911-csokonai-mihaly-vitez:
Mihaly Vitez Csokonai (1773–1805) was a Hungarian poet born at Debreczen in 1773. Educated in his native town, he was named professor of poetry there while still very young. Soon after, he lost the post for the immorality of his conduct. The last twelve years of his short life passed in near constant wretchedness. He died in his mother's house in his native town at the age of thirty-one.

The entry calls Csokonai a genial and original poet with some of the lyrical fire of Petöfi. His works include a mock-heroic poem, Dorottya, or the Triumph of the Ladies at the Carnival. He also wrote two or three comedies or farces and a number of love poems. Most of his work was published after his death, with a life, by Schedel, in the years 1844 to 1847.
britannica-1911-francia-jose-gaspar-rodr:
Jose Gaspar Rodriguez Francia (about 1757-1840), dictator of Paraguay, was born probably about 1757. One account makes him of French descent, but the truth seems to be that his father was a native of Sao Paulo in Brazil. That father came to Paraguay to run a plantation of black tobacco for the government. Francia studied theology at the college of Cordova de Tucuman and is said to have taught in that faculty. He afterwards turned to the law and practised at Asuncion, the capital of the country he would rule.

Francia won a high name at once for ability and integrity, and he was picked for important offices. When Paraguay declared independence in 1811 he became secretary to the national junta. His influence ran far beyond his nominal post. The entry follows the doctor who ruled Paraguay alone for decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-rodrig:
Alonso Rodriguez was a Spanish Jesuit, born at Valladolid in 1526, dead at Seville in 1616. He entered the Society of Jesus at twenty and taught moral theology twelve years at Monterey College. He then served twelve years as master of novices, seventeen as rector, eleven as spiritual father at Cordova. As master of novices he oversaw the celebrated theologian Francisco Suárez. His characteristics in office were care and diligence.

The book he collected from his exhortations, published at his superiors' request, was meant for his brethren but also for other religious and laymen. Of set purpose it avoids lofty mysticism and abstruse speculation, offering practical instructions on the perfect Christian life, in cloister or world. It became popular at once and remains much used. More than twenty-five editions of the Spanish original appeared, besides extracts. Over sixty French editions in seven translations appeared, twenty Italian, ten German, eight Latin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-coello:
Alonzo Coello Sánchez, born at Benifayó in 1513 or 1515, dead at Madrid in 1590, bears a Portuguese name, likely his mother's. Philip II called him his Portuguese Titian for his close connexion with Portugal. Though nothing places Sánchez in Italy, he copied Titian under Antonio Mor, his great master. In 1552 he accompanied Mor to Lisbon to paint Portuguese portraits for Charles V.

One of the earliest Spanish court portrait-painters, he grew rich on great demand. He painted Gregory XIII, Sixtus V, Spanish grandees, Cardinal Farnese, and the Dukes of Florence and Savoy. He worked at the Escorial and painted Madrid's triumphal arch for Anne of Austria's entry, wife of Philip II. His most notable portrait may be St. Ignatius Loyola, from casts taken twenty-nine years before. His greatest was his friend Father Sigüenza, engraved by Selma. His colouring resembles Titian's; his portraits are powerful, lifelike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-sanche:
Alonzo Sánchez, born at Mondéjar in 1547, died at Alcalá in 1593. He entered the Society of Jesus at Alcalá in 1565, was rector of Navalcarnero college, and in 1579 went to Mexico as seminary rector. In 1581 he sailed for the Philippines with Bishop Salazar. Sánchez, Sedeño, and a lay brother led the first Jesuits into the islands. The bishop made Sánchez counsellor and synod acts writer.

Chosen by officials, merchants, and leading citizens, Sánchez went to Madrid in 1586 as the colony's representative. His mission moved Philip II to retain the islands against advisors urging abandonment. From Madrid he went to Rome, where Sixtus V granted privileges for the Philippine Church. Gregory XIV's brief of June 1591 praised his labours, calling him a defender of the Holy See's authority and rights. Clement VIII granted favours to the islands' bishop and clergy on his request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-ferna:
Lisbon Jesuit Antonio Fernandez, born about 1569 and dead at Goa in 1642, spent his missionary life between India and Abyssinia, the old name for Ethiopia. Sent to India about 1602, he reached Abyssinia two years later and won favour with King Melek Seghed. The king, converted in 1622 after a Latin patriarch arrived at his request, publicly accepted the primacy of Rome. He made Catholicism the state religion in 1626, winning many converts, at times by force.

The king's son then backed the older faith, seized the throne in rebellion, and banned Catholic worship on pain of death. Expelled missionaries found brief shelter with a local prince, then faced ransom demands at Massowah. Fernandez, over eighty and held as a hostage, was freed when a younger companion took his place, and he returned to India. He also turned books into Ethiopian and wrote against local heresies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthazar-alv:
Balthazar Alvarez was a Spanish mystic and the spiritual director of St Teresa, born at Cervera in 1533, who died at Belmonte in 1580. He studied philosophy and theology at Alcalá, and by eighteen was already remarkable for prayer and piety. Drawn first to the Carthusians' contemplative life, he instead entered the Society of Jesus at Alcalá in 1555.

Interrupted studies slowed his scholastic theology, but prayer made him eminent in mystical theology instead. Made priest in 1558, he was entrusted at twenty-five with Teresa's direction as she founded the Discalced Carmelites. He guided her spirit, defended her from critics, encouraged her reform, and helped frame its rules. Late in life his prayer method was questioned as a devil's delusion, but the Jesuit General approved it while barring general use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-alloue:
Claude Allouez, a famous Jesuit missionary and explorer of the American West, was born in France in 1620 and died in 1689 near the Saint John's river in Indiana. Shea calls him the West's Catholicity founder. He laboured with Marquette after teaching as a professor. A surviving prayer book in Illinois and French is said to have been prepared by Allouez for Marquette's use.

He worked among the Indians for thirty-two years and preached to twenty different tribes. He is said to have baptised ten thousand neophytes with his own hand. He put the Kaskaskia mission on a firm basis after Marquette's death forced him to leave it. No missionary of his time dared more or travelled wider: he reached the western end of Lake Superior. He became the United States' first vicar-general, appointed by Laval of Quebec over the whole western country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crisostomo-he:
A biographical entry follows Crisostomo Henriquez, a Cistercian of the Spanish Congregation, born at Madrid in 1594 and dead at Louvain in 1632. Entering the monastery of Huerta at thirteen, he studied philosophy and theology in several houses, showing an early taste for historical research. While still a student he published a history of the monastery of Meyra.

Sent to the Low Countries at his parents' request, he was ordered to write the Cistercian Order's history. He visited the great Flemish abbeys of Aulnes, Villers, and Dunes, consulting libraries and archives. From 1619 until his death he published over forty works, becoming historian of his congregation, then its vicar-general, and finally grand prior of Calatrava's military order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-alvarez:
Diego Alvarez was a Spanish Dominican theologian born about 1550. He taught theology for twenty years in Burgos, Trianos, Plasencia, and Valladolid. Then he taught for ten years at the Minerva in Rome. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his part in the great dispute over grace that flared when Molina published his Concordia in 1588.

Before the Congregation de Auxiliis set up by the pope, Alvarez defended the teaching of Thomas Aquinas. He stood alone for three years and then beside Thomas de Lemos until the hearings were suspended in 1606. Named archbishop of Trani that same year, he spent his last years there writing defenses of Aquinas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-rodrigu:
Diego Rodriguez de Silva y Velazquez was born at Seville in 1599. He took his mother's name and trained first under Herrera, whose temper drove him away. Then he studied under Pacheco, whose school led the city. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows the young painter to Madrid in 1622, where friends at court opened the royal collections to him.

Called back by Philip the Fourth, he painted the king and rose in court favor. Later he traveled to Italy, where he painted the slave Juan de Pareja and Pope Innocent the Tenth. His late masterworks, The Spinners and The Maids of Honour, crown a career the entry presents as the highest point of Spanish painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-banez:
Domingo Banez, more properly Vanez, was a Spanish Dominican theologian born on 29 February 1528 at Medina del Campo. At fifteen he began philosophy at Salamanca, took the Dominican habit three years later, and professed in 1547. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names his teachers, Melchior Cano, Diego de Chaves, and Pedro Sotomayor, under whom he built the learning and acumen that made him famous.

Banez became the great champion of Thomist teaching on grace against Molina, and his name marks the whole school of Bañezianism. The entry lists his works and the later writers who debated him, from Gayraud to Regnon. He died at his birthplace on 22 October 1604, a master of the schools at the height of Spanish theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enrique-flore:
Enrique Florez was a Spanish theologian, archaeologist, and historian, born at Valladolid in 1701 and dead at Madrid in 1773. He joined the Augustinians in 1715 while very young. He gave his whole life to works on history and antiquities that remain valuable for Spain's civil and church history. One of the most learned men Spain produced, he enjoyed the respect of the eminent men of his time.

His chief work, Espana Sagrada, a geographical and historical theatre of the Church in Spain, followed the model of the Gallia Christiana and the Italia Sacra. In fifty-one volumes it tells the Church's history in Spain with bishops' lives, enriched by ancient documents found nowhere else. Florez himself wrote and published only twenty-nine volumes before his death. Two fellow Augustinians, Risco and Fernandez, finished the rest. His Llave Historial of 1743 beat the French Art of Verifying Dates, which did not appear until 1750.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enrique-henri:
Enrique Henriquez was a noted Jesuit theologian, born at Oporto in 1536 and dead at Tivoli in 1608. At sixteen, in 1552, he entered the Society of Jesus and soon won fame for learning in philosophy and theology. He taught both subjects at Cordova and Salamanca, where Francisco Suarez and Gregory of Valencia sat among his pupils. In 1593 he left the Society for the Dominicans, but soon came back.

The break came after censors disapproved passages he had printed in a preface, and Superior General Acquaviva ordered the page torn out. Disturbed by the punishment, Henriquez got leave to join the Dominicans, then took Gregory of Valencia's advice and returned. His Summa of Moral Theology, issued at Salamanca in 1591 and 1593, was banned in 1603 until corrected. It allowed confession by letter, though not absolution, and held views unfavourable to the Church's rights. Saint Alphonsus prized his authority on moral questions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faustus-of-ri:
Faustus of Riez was a fifth-century bishop and defender of Semipelagianism. Born in Britain, he entered the monastery of Lerins and became abbot. As bishop of Riez he kept his ascetic life and founded monasteries. Exiled eight years by the Visigothic king Euric, he returned after Euric's death.

Faustus opposed both Pelagius and the harsh doctrine of predestination. At the bishops' request he wrote two books on grace and free will. The work leaned Semipelagian and was condemned at Orange in 529. He also held the soul corporeal in a sense, God alone being pure spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-sua:
Francisco Suarez, called Doctor Eximius, the extraordinary doctor, was born at Granada on 5 January 1548 and died at Lisbon on 25 September 1617. He was a Jesuit theologian whom Paul V praised as pious and eminent. He entered the Society at Salamanca in 1564, studied philosophy and theology there, and was ordained in 1572. He taught at Avila, Segovia, Valladolid, Rome, Alcala, Salamanca, and Coimbra, where Philip II sent him to give prestige to the university and where he taught from 1597 to 1616.

Gregory XIII attended his first lecture at Rome. Paul V asked him to answer the errors of King James of England and wished to keep him nearby. The doctors of Barcelona went out to meet him with their faculty insignia. His writings, deep, penetrating, and clear, show remarkable knowledge of the Fathers and of heretical and church writers alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-xim:
Francisco Ximenez de Cisneros, often spelled Jimenez, was a Franciscan cardinal and Primate of Spain. He was born at Torrelaguna in New Castile in 1436 and dead at Roa near Valladolid in 1517. Educated at Alcala and Salamanca in canon and civil law, he practised at Rome as a consistorial advocate. Sixtus IV promised him the first vacant benefice at home, the post of Uzeda, which Archbishop Carrillo of Toledo wanted for another man.

Released in 1480, he became grand vicar of Siguenza, then in 1484 joined the Observant Franciscans at Toledo, served as guardian at Salzeda, and became provincial of Castile. In 1492 Cardinal Mendoza made him confessor to Queen Isabella, on condition he still live as a monk. In 1495 he succeeded Mendoza as Archbishop of Toledo and Primate of Spain. He reformed his order, founded Alcala University, and served as regent of Castile after Ferdinand's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-telle:
Gabriel Téllez, a Spanish priest and poet better known as Tirso de Molina, created Don Juan. Born at Madrid around 1571 and schooled at Alcalá, he joined the Mercedarian order. He held its offices, from superior at Trujillo in 1619 to prior at Soria, where he died in 1648. Little else is known of his early years.

Tirso's first book, The Cigarrales of Toledo of 1624, mixed tales, poems, and comedies in the manner of Boccaccio's Decameron. He is credited with four hundred plays, though only about eighty survive, issued in five parts during his life. His fame rests on The Trickster of Seville, where Don Juan first walks the stage, later reborn in Mozart's opera and Byron's poem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-vasqu:
Gabriel Vasquez, a Jesuit theologian born near Belmonte around 1550, was called by Benedict XIV the luminary of theology. He entered the Society at Alcalá in 1569, taught moral theology at Ocaña, Madrid, and Alcalá, and, before turning thirty, was called to Rome to teach at the Roman College. After six years there he returned to Alcalá and taught until his death in 1604.

Vasquez knew the schools and Fathers deeply, above all Augustine and Thomas, and wrote with clarity and strict method. His private views set him apart at times: natural law rooted in reason itself, divine ideas as God's knowledge of possible creatures, and grace as every good impulse urging right action. The Duke of Lerma sought his counsel on the gravest affairs of Philip III's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-lainez:
James Lainez, also spelled Laynez, was the Jesuits' second general and a theologian. He was born at Almazán, Castile, in 1512 and died at Rome on 19 January 1565. His family, Christian for many generations, descended from Jewish stock, as Sacchini established. Lainez graduated in arts at Alcalá in 1531. He won his philosophy licentiate there at twenty in 1532. At Alcalá he and his friend Salmerón heard of Ignatius Loyola.

To meet Ignatius they went to Paris university in 1533 and fell under his masterful will. Lainez was the second to join Loyola. He was one of seven who vowed religious life on 15 August 1534 in Montmartre's St Denis chapel. Three years followed in charity and zeal, mostly in northern Italy. In 1537 Ignatius sent his companions to press onward in their mission. The entry opens the life of Loyola's closest theological heir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joao-rodrigue:
João Rodriguez, a Portuguese Jesuit missionary and author born at Alcochete in 1558 and dead in Japan in 1633. He joined the Society in 1576 and began Japan mission work in 1583. Esteem from the ruler Hideyoshi eased his path, and he threw himself into Japanese study.

Rodriguez made the tongue open to the West. His Japanese grammar, printed at Nagasaki in 1604, was abridged at Macao in 1624, and a French edition followed from a Paris manuscript in 1825. His Japanese-Portuguese dictionary of 1603, later adapted into French, ranks among the great linguistic fruits of the Jesuit mission and still aids scholars of early Japanese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-bernardo:
Jose Bernardo Sanchez was a Spanish Franciscan missionary in California who fought the secularization of the missions. Born at Robledillo in Old Castile in 1778, he became a Franciscan in 1794 and joined the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico in 1803. He reached California the next year, serving at San Diego, Purisima, and San Gabriel.

As chaplain he joined a military expedition in 1806 and explored the interior for new mission sites in 1821. From 1827 to 1831 he reluctantly served as president of the missions and vicar forane, dreading the superior's office. His appeals for relief were granted at last, but he lived only two more years. In office he fought Governor Echeandia's secularization plan, arguing in critical notes that it would destroy the missions and ruin the neophytes. The sight of that ruin hastened his death in 1833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-fernande:
Juan Fernández was a Spanish Jesuit lay brother who carried the Gospel to Japan. Born at Cordova, he sailed with St. Francis Xavier's party, named in Xavier's Malacca letter of June 1549. In Japan he traveled with Xavier to Hirado, Yamaguchi, and Kyoto, then stayed at Yamaguchi with Father Cosmo Torres when Xavier left for China.

Fernández won debates with Japanese scholars on God, creation, and the soul's immortality, drawing the anger of Buddhist priests. Xavier praised his fluent Japanese and his clear translations of Torres' teaching. His humility under insult converted a brilliant young doctor who became a Jesuit light. He compiled the first Japanese grammar and lexicon and died in Japan in 1567.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-perez:
Juan Pérez was the Franciscan guardian of La Rábida who helped Columbus sail. Once accountant to the Queen of Spain and later Isabella's confessor, Pérez retired to the little convent near Palos, where he became guardian. There, in 1484 or 1485, Columbus met him and the cosmographer Antonio de Marchena, long confused with Pérez by later writers.

When Columbus, footsore and dispirited, meant to carry his plan to France, Pérez persuaded him to consult Isabella first. At the queen's invitation Pérez pleaded the navigator's cause, and Columbus later wrote that only two friars stayed faithful when all others mocked him. Pérez died before 1513, his convent now a national museum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manoel-alvare:
Manoel Alvarez was a Jesuit educator born on Madeira in 1526 and dead at Evora in 1582. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1546. He taught classical languages with great success. He served as rector of the colleges of Coimbra and Evora.

Among more than three hundred Jesuits who wrote language textbooks, he ranks first. His Latin grammar became the standard work under the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum. Sommervogel lists about four hundred editions of the whole work or parts, printed in Europe, Asia, and America. Translations ran to Bohemian, Croatian, Flemish, French, German, Hungarian, Illyrian, Italian, Polish, and Spanish. A Chinese version appeared at Shanghai in 1869, and a Japanese version in 1594. More than a grammar, it taught Latin method, though later critics faulted its Latin text and order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natchez:
Mississippi makes up the diocese of Natchez, erected 28 July 1837. Missionary work by Catholics in the region started with the journeys of Marquette, La Salle, and Iberville. Iberville set up a settlement amid the Natchez people and put up Fort Rosalie where the present city stands. Capuchins, Jesuits, and secular clergy worked at Biloxi, Natchez, and Yazoo.

The missions' early years brought martyrdom: secular priests Saint Cosme and Foucault died at Indian hands, as did Jesuits Du Poisson, Souart, and Senat. Then, in 1787, McKenna, White, and Savage, three priests out of Salamanca, made their home at Natchez and built hopeful missions in the town and its neighbourhood. Spain's handover of the land to the United States left those missions all but deserted, their property gone, and bids to win it back fruitless. Natchez Catholics relied for years on priests who happened to pass through, until Bishop Chanche came in 1841.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rodez:
Rodez is a diocese in southern France matching the department of Aveyron, once Rouergue. United to Cahors by the Concordat of 1802, it became a see again by the Concordat of 1817 and bull of 1822. It held old Rodez minus the deanery of Saint Antonin, old Vabres, and a few Cahors communes. Tradition credits St Martial with founding its church and the Ceignac sanctuary.

Bishops appear before 675, when Sidonius Apollinaris notes Goths leaving the city bishopless. Amantius, late in the fifth century, is the first named. Later bishops include Quintianus, later of Clermont, and Dalmatius. Jean de Cardaillac, Patriarch of Alexandria, fought English rule. Francis d'Estaing served as ambassador to Julius II. Louis Avelly wrote the life of St Vincent de Paul. Joseph Bourret was made cardinal in 1893. The cathedral, Gothic of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, is famed for its belfry of 1510-26 and rood-beam. Milhau turned Calvinist in 1534.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seez:
The diocese of Séez, made to match the French department of Orne when it was restored under the Concordat of 1802, is the subject of this long local history. Its early bishop list cannot be trusted before 900, the entry warns. It names the shadowy first bishops anyway. It identifies Passivus, present at councils after 533, as the first bishop known with certainty.

Later bishops, saints, shrines, and pilgrimages fill the rest. Séez had a twelfth-century cathedral. Its famed shrines of Our Lady drew pilgrims from far off. The Grande Trappe of Soligny survived there. Teaching and nursing sisterhoods founded in the diocese are also covered. Closing figures count 326,952 inhabitants at the Concordat's end in 1905, with 45 parishes and 467 branch churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alphonsus-:
St. Alphonsus Rodriguez, also called Alonso, was a Jesuit lay brother born at Segovia in Spain on 25 July 1532 and dead at Majorca on 31 October 1617. This entry first warns readers not to confuse him with Father Rodriguez, author of Christian Perfection, eminent in holiness but never canonized, a mix-up the similarity of names invites.

Son of a wool merchant reduced to poverty while Alfonso was young. He married Mary Francisco Suarez at twenty-six, was widowed at thirty-one with one surviving child, and turned to prayer and mortification. After his third child's death he sought religious life, and through earlier contact with Peter Faber and the first Jesuits in Spain, he entered the Society at forty as a lay brother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-gonz:
Peter Gonzalez, popularly St Elmo, preached to sailors and soldiers along the coasts of Spain. Born at Astorga in 1190 and schooled by his uncle, bishop of Astorga, who gave him a canonry young, he joined the Dominicans and became a renowned preacher. Crowds gathered for his sermons, and conversions followed in great numbers.

He accompanied Ferdinand III of León on campaigns against the Moors, but his heart lay with preaching to the poor. He spent his later years instructing the ignorant and mariners of Galicia and the Spanish coast. He died at Tuy on 15 April 1246 and lies buried in its cathedral. Never formally canonised, his cult was confirmed in 1741, and St Elmo's fire bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-sanche:
Thomas Sanchez, a Jesuit moral theologian born at Cordova in 1550, became famous, and much attacked, for his great work on marriage. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1567, after first being refused over a speech impediment that he prayed to be freed from before an image of Our Lady at Cordova. He served for a time as master of novices at Granada, then gave his life to writing.

His Disputationes de Sancti Matrimonii Sacramento, whose first volume appeared at Genoa in 1602, treated the sacrament of marriage in exhaustive detail. Contemporaries praised his penitential zeal and his unbroken baptismal innocence, and his director testified to a life of steady self-discipline. He died at the college of Granada in May 1610 of inflammation of the lungs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zeferino-gonz:
Zeferino Gonzalez was a Spanish Dominican cardinal, theologian, and philosopher, born at Villoria in Oviedo province on 28 January 1831. He died at Madrid's Dominican Convent of La Pasion on 29 November 1894. He entered the Dominicans on 28 November 1844, took solemn vows a year later, and was sent to Manila in 1848 to finish his studies. He became lector of philosophy in January 1853 and priest the following year.

In 1874 he was named Bishop of Malaga, but before taking charge he was consecrated Bishop of Cordova in October 1875. Eight years later he moved to Seville's archiepiscopal see, and in November 1884 Leo XIII made him cardinal of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. In May 1885 he gained Spain's primacy, the Patriarchate of the Indies, the army vicar-generalship, and the royal chapel's major chaplaincy. In December 1889 he resigned all but the cardinalate and spent his last five years in study and prayer.
george-walker-at-suez:
Anthony Trollope cast a plain London businessman as hero of George Walker at Suez, a short tale from Tales of All Countries. George Walker of Friday Street narrates his own adventure with honesty. Sent to Cairo for a sore throat, he suspects his partners wanted him out of the firm. Lonely hotel days in Egypt humble a man who craved homage.

Suez itself disgusts him: sand, heat, no water, and a cavernous hotel stripped of comforts. One day of that dull week, though, lends a halo to the trip in his memory. Passengers bound for Australia sweep through Cairo and Suez in flocks between steamers and trains. Among strangers, Walker tastes the respect and notice that London never gave him. Trollope keeps the scale tiny and the irony gentle. Readers who enjoy quiet character comedy, where a nobody's pride takes a holiday, will savor this brief Egyptian episode.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AlvarezLuisDr_D: Dr. Luis Alvarez was a Nobel Prize-winning physicist who turned his science on the Kennedy assassination, testing what the Zapruder film and the physics of the shots could prove. This file holds the government material filed under his name in the assassination records. Alvarez's experiments, including his famous work on the head shot's movement, made him the best-known scientist in the case. The file is kept as issued, part of the record of science entering the assassination debate.
